subtitle: Della Vedova (2026) says the price you pay decides who profits, not the side you pick. We ran his four tests on our own sealed Kalshi tape — 17 days, the whole exchange, six market families kept strictly separate.
tiles: what liquidity takers lost, net of fees, in 15 settled days across the six families
what liquidity makers made over the same prints, net of maker fees
what Kalshi took in fees — more than the entire maker profit pool it sits beside
what ten points of extra forecasting accuracy is worth at 50¢ versus at 95¢
body:
What replicates, and what does not.

  ①  The paper's headline mechanism replicates almost exactly. A ten-point gain in directional accuracy is worth 11.8–13.5¢ per contract when price sits at 50¢ and 0.5–1.8¢ once price reaches 95¢ (paper: 11.6¢ → 1.5¢). The interaction coefficient is −2.31 to −2.89 across our six families against the paper's −2.244, on a different exchange, a different asset mix and a different year. Being right stops paying once the price has already moved; arriving early is what pays.

  ②  The benchmark-contamination result replicates cleanly. Regress execution edge on directional edge and the coefficient is −0.10 to −0.34 under a backward-VWAP reference price, and −0.000 to −0.037 once the reference is a single adjacent print (paper: −0.178 → 0.000). The apparent trade-off between picking well and executing well is an artifact of scoring flow against a benchmark built from that same flow.

  ③  The inversion does not replicate in the paper's form, and the reason is instructive. Polymarket retail picks winners 51.3% of the time and still loses. Our takers pick the winning side only 42–49% of the time (contract-weighted) — they lose on the side picked as well as on the price paid, because Kalshi taker flow is tilted hard into cheap longshots. Same conclusion, blunter: the profitable role is not the accurate one.

  ④  Kalshi has a fee, and Polymarket did not. That single difference dominates our tape: takers pay 0.6–1.1¢ per contract, which is larger than the entire gross edge the makers on the other side of those same prints collect. Kalshi's fee take, $122M in 15 days, exceeds every dollar the maker side kept.
implications:
For our own book — what these numbers say we should do.

  ▸  Quote where the maker edge survives its own fee. Crypto 15-minute (+0.27¢/contract, 95% CI [0.11, 0.44]) and crypto hourly/daily (+0.47¢, CI [0.25, 0.68]) are the two books where the maker edge is both positive and tight across markets — and Kalshi charges no maker fee there. That is a per-market-repeatable edge, not a handful of lucky markets.

  ▸  Read the maker-fee list before quoting a sports book. Kalshi charges makers 0.0175·p·(1−p) on ~80 listed series and nothing elsewhere. On KXATPMATCH the maker fee (0.277¢) is the whole gross edge (0.271¢) — net zero. On KXWTAMATCH the net is −0.34¢. Sports game maker edge is +0.39¢ gross but +0.18¢ after fee, with a confidence interval straddling zero.

  ▸  Do not read the big sports-prop maker profit as an edge. It is +$99M, but 78% of it sits in five series (World Cup outright, UFC fights, World Cup goal markets) and the per-market interval is [−0.85, +4.35]¢ — that is a favourite–longshot windfall in a few crowded books, not a strategy. The paper hits the same wall: its top-10 bot wallets earn 70% of all bot profit.

  ▸  Stop quoting into the close. Maker edge decays monotonically toward expiry and turns negative in the final minutes — crypto 15-min goes +0.66¢ (10–60 min out) → +0.26¢ (5–10 min) → +0.01¢ (2–5 min) → −0.35¢ (under 2 min). The last band is where our fills are worth least and our adverse selection is worst. Whatever we quote there needs a materially wider spread or no quote at all.

  ▸  Stop scoring our own execution against a VWAP we helped set. Every execution-quality number we produce from a backward VWAP built out of our own prints carries the bias measured on page 5. Use the adjacent print, or a forward window that skips our own fills.
caveats: Caveats, stated plainly. ▸ Kalshi's public tape carries no trader identity, so the paper's wallet-level classification (bot / sophisticated / retail / casual) and its within-wallet persistence tests cannot be run at all; our axis is the order role recorded on each print, which is the paper's own mechanism margin, not its classification margin. ▸ With two roles per print the maker's components are the exact mirror of the taker's, so "maker vs taker" here is one comparison, not two independent populations. ▸ Settlement truth comes from a catalog snapshot taken 2026-07-24T21:30Z: crypto and sports join at 98–100%, politics at 79% and economics at 60%, so those two families are selected toward markets that resolved early — read them as indicative. ▸ For the four high-volume families the backward-VWAP benchmark is rebuilt each day rather than across a market's whole life; their markets are intraday, so this costs each market its opening print. ▸ Fees are modelled continuously from the published July 7 2026 schedule (taker 0.07·p·(1−p), maker 0.0175·p·(1−p) on listed series only); Kalshi rounds up per order, so the true taker cost is a shade higher than shown. ▸ Markout uses subsequent trade prints, not quotes.
